According to the [[World Prison Brief]] (WPB) the United States had the world's highest incarceration rate from 2001 (when the US overtook Russia) through October 4, 2022 (US rate of 629 per 100,000 population at that time). That was except for periods when the [[Seychelles]] (population around 121,000) had the highest rate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Walmsley |first1=Roy |title=Global Incarceration and Prison Trends {{!}} Office of Justice Programs |journal=Forum on Crime and Society |volume=3 |issue=1 & 2 |pages=65–78 |date=December 2003 |url=https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/global-incarceration-and-prison-trends}} NCJ number 207373. See [https://www.unodc.org/pdf/crime/forum/forum3_Art3.pdf full text].</ref><ref name=WorldPrisonBriefhighestlowest>[http://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest Highest to Lowest - Prison Population Total]. From [[World Prison Brief]] (WPB). See [http://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison_population_rate?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All rates list]. See [https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison-population-total?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All counts list]. Data for many countries in the rates and counts lists can be one to several years old because that is the latest data available, or the latest that has been vetted. Use dropdown menu to choose lists of countries by region, or the whole world. Use menu to select highest-to-lowest lists of prison population totals, prison population rates, percentage of pre-trial detainees / remand prisoners, percentage of female prisoners, percentage of foreign prisoners, and occupancy rate. "We do not include juvenile imprisonment data in the highest to lowest lists." Column headings in WPB tables can be clicked to reorder columns lowest to highest, or alphabetically. For detailed information for each country click on any country name in lists. The individual country pages also give the date and year of the data. See also the [http://www.prisonstudies.org/world-prison-brief-data WPB main data page] and click on the map links and/or the sidebar links to get to the region and country desired. See these [[Wayback Machine|Wayback]] archives for lists from previous years: [https://web.archive.org/web/20250000000000*/https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison-population-total?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All count lists] and [https://web.archive.org/web/20250000000000*/http://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest rate lists].</ref><ref>[[World Prison Brief]] rates list: [https://web.archive.org/web/20221004022605/https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison_population_rate?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All Archive of October 4, 2022].</ref><ref>[[World Prison Brief]] rates list: [https://web.archive.org/web/20221012111650/https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison_population_rate?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All Archive of October 12, 2022]. That is the next available WPB archive after the Oct 4 one. That was when 2020 data for the US became publicly available, and so the US dropped from the highest rate to the sixth highest rate.</ref><ref name=WPB-USA>[http://www.prisonstudies.org/country/united-states-america United States of America]. [[World Prison Brief]]. See tables and graphs for timelines of US rates and counts. Juvenile numbers are listed here, but are not included in the highest to lowest lists according to the [https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison-population-total lists main page].</ref><ref name=WPB-Russia>[http://www.prisonstudies.org/country/Russian_Federation Russian Federation]. [[World Prison Brief]]. See tables and graphs for timelines of rates and counts.</ref><ref>[[World Prison Brief]] rates list: [https://web.archive.org/web/20140717094005/https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison_population_rate?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All Archive of July 17, 2014]. Example of when the [[Seychelles]] had the highest rate.</ref> According to the WPB as of September 3, 2025 the United States had the fifth highest incarceration rate in the world, at 541 per 100,000 population, using the latest available solid US numbers (2022) from the [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]].<ref name=WorldPrisonBriefhighestlowest/><ref name=WPB-USA/><ref>[[World Prison Brief]] rates list: [https://web.archive.org/web/20250903204131/https://www.prisonstudies.org/highest-to-lowest/prison_population_rate?field_region_taxonomy_tid=All Archive of September 3, 2025].</ref> Between 2019 and 2020, the United States saw a significant drop in the total number of incarcerations. State and federal prison, and local jail, incarcerations dropped from 2.1&nbsp;million in 2019 to 1.7&nbsp;million in 2020. The US incarceration total has risen since 2020. See the [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] timeline table to the right below the map.<ref name=BJS-timeline/> 

As of their March 2023 publication, the [[Prison Policy Initiative]], a non-profit organization for [[Decarceration in the United States|decarceration]], estimated that in the United States, about 1.9&nbsp;million people were or are currently incarcerated. Of those who were incarcerated, 1,047,000 people were in state prison, 514,000 in local jails, 209,000 in federal prisons, 36,000 in youth correctional facilities, 34,000 in immigration detention camps, 22,000 in involuntary commitment, 8,000 in territorial prisons, 2,000 in Indian Country jails, and 1,000 in United States military prisons. The data is from various years depending on what is the latest available data.<ref>[https://www.prisonpolicy.org/reports/pie2023.html Mass Incarceration: The Whole Pie 2023]. By Wendy Sawyer and Peter Wagner. March 14, 2023. [[Prison Policy Initiative]].</ref>

Corrections (which includes prisons, jails, probation, and parole) cost around $74&nbsp;billion in 2007 according to the [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]] (BJS).<ref name="bjscosts">[https://web.archive.org/web/20120101181331/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/glance/tables/exptyptab.cfm Direct expenditures by justice function, 1982–2007 (billions of dollars)]. Inflation adjusted to 2007 dollars. [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]] (BJS). Retrieved January 1, 2012, by the [[Internet Archive]]. See [https://web.archive.org/web/20120101082347/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/glance/exptyp.cfm BJS timeline graph based on the data].</ref><ref name="bjscosts2">[http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=2192 Justice Expenditures and Employment, FY 1982–2007 – Statistical Tables] (NCJ 236218). Published December 2011. [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]] (BJS). By Tracey Kyckelhahn, PhD, BJS statistician. See table 2 of the [http://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/jee8207st.pdf PDF]. "Total justice expenditures, by justice function, FY 1982–2007 (real dollars)". A total of around $74&nbsp;billion for corrections in 2007.</ref> According to the ''Justice Expenditures and Employment in the United States, 2017'' report release by BJS, it is estimated that county and municipal governments spent roughly US$30&nbsp;billion on corrections in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Justice Expenditures and Employment in the United States, 2017|url=https://bjs.ojp.gov/library/publications/justice-expenditures-and-employment-united-states-2017|access-date=2021-07-27|website=Bureau of Justice Statistics|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=July 2021|title=Justice Expenditures and Employment in the United States, 2017|url=https://bjs.ojp.gov/sites/g/files/xyckuh236/files/media/document/jeeus17.pdf|website=U.S. Department of Justice; Office of Justice Programs; Bureau of Justice Statistics}}</ref>

== Prison and jail population ==
[[File:US incarceration timeline-clean.svg|thumb|300px|Total incarceration in the United States by year]]
[[File:US adult correctional population timeline.gif|thumb|300px|Total US incarceration peaked in 2008. Total correctional population peaked in 2007.<ref name=cpus2013/>]]
[[File:US incarceration and correctional population rates over time.jpg|thumb|300px|US incarceration and correctional population rates over time. The incarceration rate peaked in 2008.<ref name=cpusa2015>[https://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=5870 Correctional Populations in the United States, 2015]. By Danielle Kaeble and Lauren Glaze, ''BJS Statisticians.'' Dec. 2016. [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]]. See [https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/cpus15.pdf PDF]. See table 4 on page 4: "Rate of persons supervised by U.S. adult correctional systems, by correctional status, 2000 and 2005–2015".</ref>]]
{{See also|List of U.S. states by incarceration rate}}

Total U.S. incarceration (prisons and jails) peaked in 2008 at 2.31&nbsp;million. Total correctional population peaked in 2007 at 7.34&nbsp;million: in prison, jail, on [[probation]], or on [[parole]] (released from prison with restrictions). See [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] table to the right after the graph.<ref name=cpus2013>[http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=5177 Correctional Populations in the United States, 2013] (NCJ 248479). Published December 2014 by [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]] (BJS). By Lauren E. Glaze and Danielle Kaeble, BJS statisticians. See appendix table 5 on page 13 in the [http://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/cpus13.pdf PDF], for "Estimated number of persons supervised by adult correctional systems, by correctional status, 2000–2013."</ref><ref name=BJStrends>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090831081336/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs//glance/tables/corr2tab.htm Correctional Populations]. Table covering 1980 to 2007. [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]].</ref> 

Counting all inmates (not just those in prisons and jails) brings the number at the beginning of 2008 to 2.42 million inmates. This is by adding in inmates in [[Territories of the United States|U.S. territories]], military facilities, [[U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) owned and contracted facilities ([[Immigration detention in the United States|immigration detention]]), jails in [[Indian country]], and [[Youth incarceration in the United States|juvenile facilities]]. That means the United States had around 24.7% of the world's 9.8&nbsp;million prisoners.<ref name=prisoners2008>''[http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=1763 Prisoners in 2008] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716170211/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=1763 |date=July 16, 2011 }}.'' (NCJ 228417). December 2009 report from the [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]]. By William J. Sabol, PhD and Heather C. West, PhD, BJS Statisticians. Also, Matthew Cooper, BJS Intern. Table 9 on page 8 of the [http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/p08.pdf PDF file] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716170001/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/p08.pdf |date=July 16, 2011 }} has the number of inmates in state or federal prison facilities, local jails, U.S. territories, military facilities, ICE owned and contracted facilities, jails in Indian country, and juvenile facilities (2006 Census of Juveniles in Residential Placement). Table 8 on page 8 has the incarceration rates for 2000, 2007, and 2008.</ref><ref name=icps8/><ref name=cjrp>Sickmund, M., Sladky, T.J., Kang, W., & Puzzanchera, C. [http://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/ezacjrp/ Easy Access to the Census of Juveniles in Residential Placement]. Click "National Crosstabs" at the top, and then choose the census years. Click "Show table" to get the total number of juvenile inmates for those years. Or go '''[http://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/ezacjrp/asp/display.asp here]''' for all the years. [[Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention]].</ref> See chart below:
[[File:Total US inmates 2007-8.gif|none|300px]]

A [[Pew Research Center|Pew]] report released February 28, 2008 indicated that more than 1 in 100 adults in the United States were in prison or jail at the beginning of 2008:<ref name=pewcenterstudy>{{cite web |title=One in 100: Behind Bars in America 2008 |url=https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/reports/2008/02/28/one-in-100-behind-bars-in-america-2008 |website=pew.org |publisher=[[The Pew Charitable Trusts|The Pew Center on the States]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130903085218/http://www.pewstates.org/uploadedFiles/PCS_Assets/2008/one%20in%20100.pdf |archive-date=Sep 3, 2013 |language=en |date=Feb 28, 2008 |url-status=live}} See [https://www.pew.org/-/media/legacy/uploadedfiles/pcs_assets/2008/one20in20100pdf.pdf full text].</ref>

{{quote|
With 1,596,127 in state or federal prison custody, and another 723,131 in local jails, the total adult inmate count at the beginning of 2008 stood at 2,319,258. With the number of adults just shy of 230 million, the actual incarceration rate is 1 in every 99.1 adults.
}}

In 2008, the United States had the highest documented incarceration rate in the world, at 760 per 100,000.<ref name=cpus2013/><ref name=WPB-USA/><ref name=cpusa2012>{{cite web|title= Lauren E. Glaze and Errin J. Herberman, Ph.D., Correctional Population in the United States, 2012, Bureau of Justice Statistics (December 2013) Rates|url=http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=4843}}</ref><ref name=WorldPrisonBriefhighestlowest/> However, following over a decade of [[Decarceration in the United States|decarceration]], the prison and jail population declined from a 2008 peak of 2.3&nbsp;million to 1.7&nbsp;million (505 per 100,000) in 2020.<ref name=WPB-USA/><ref name=BJS-timeline/>

In the last quarter of the twentieth century, the incarceration rate in the US increased by 325 percent.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sentencingproject.org/issues/incarceration/|title=Incarceration {{!}} The Sentencing Project|website=The Sentencing Project|language=en-US|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref> Between the years 2001 and 2012, crime rates (both property and violent crimes) have declined 22% after already falling 30% in years prior between 1991 and 2001.<ref name="brookings.edu">{{Cite news|url=https://www.brookings.edu/research/ten-economic-facts-about-crime-and-incarceration-in-the-united-states/|title=Ten Economic Facts about Crime and Incarceration in the United States {{!}} Brookings Institution|date=May 1, 2014|newspaper=Brookings|language=en-US|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref> In 2012, 710 out of every 100,000 U.S. residents were imprisoned in either local jails, state prisons, federal prisons, or privately operated facilities,<ref name="brookings.edu"/> representing close to a quarter of the global prison population.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://scholarworks.sjsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1037&context=themis|title=Themis: Research Journal of Justice Studies and Forensic Science|last=Hanna|first=Peter|date=May 10, 2016|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://qz.com/458675/in-america-mass-incarceration-has-caused-more-crime-than-its-prevented/|title=In America, mass incarceration has caused more crime than it's prevented|last=Schrager|first=Allison|newspaper=Quartz|language=en-US|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref>

The [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] has released a study which finds that, despite the total number of prisoners incarcerated for drug-related offenses increasing by 57,000 between 1997 and 2004, the proportion of drug offenders to total prisoners in State prison populations stayed steady at 21%. The percentage of Federal prisoners serving time for drug offenses declined from 63% in 1997 to 55% in that same period.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090830192737/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/pub/pdf/dudsfp04.pdf Christopher J. Mumola: Drug Use and Dependence, State and Federal Prisoners, 2004, U.S. Department of Justice, October 2006, NCJ 213530]</ref> In the twenty-five years since the passage of the [[Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986]], the United States penal population rose from around 300,000 to more than two million.<ref>{{cite book|last=Alexander|first=Michelle|title=The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness|year=2010|publisher=The New Press|location=New York|page=6|title-link=The New Jim Crow}}</ref> Between 1986 and 1991, African-American women's incarceration in state prisons for drug offenses increased by 828 percent.<ref>{{cite book|last=Golden|first=Renny|title=War on the Family: Mothers in Prison and the Families They Leave Behind|year=2005|publisher=Taylor and Friends|location=New York|page=46}}</ref>

In 2009, the [[U.S. Department of Justice]] announced that the growth rate of the state prison population had fallen to its lowest since 2006, but it still had a 0.2% growth-rate compared to the total U.S. prison population.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/py09ac.pdf |title=US DOJ Data Brief: Prisoners at Yearend 2009–Advance Counts}}</ref> The [[Prisons in California|California state prison system]] population fell in 2009, the first year that populations had fallen in 38 years.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.aolnews.com/nation/article/us-state-prison-population-falls-for-first-time-in-38-years/19403469 |title=US State Prison Population Falls for First Time in 38 Years |last=Martelle |first=Scott |year=2010 |publisher=AOL |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100322200340/http://www.aolnews.com/nation/article/us-state-prison-population-falls-for-first-time-in-38-years/19403469 |archive-date=2010-03-22 }}</ref>

When looking at specific populations within the criminal justice system the growth rates are vastly different. In 1977, there were just slightly more than eleven thousand incarcerated women. By 2004, the number of [[Incarceration of women in the United States|women under state or federal prison]] had increased by 757 percent, to more than 111,000, and the percentage of women in prison has increased every year, at roughly double the rate of men, since 2000.<ref>{{cite book|last=Talvi|first=Silja J.A|title=Women Behind Bars: The Crisis of Women in the U.S Prison System|url=https://archive.org/details/womenbehindbarsc00talv|url-access=registration|year=2007|publisher=Seal Press|location=California|page=[https://archive.org/details/womenbehindbarsc00talv/page/3 3]|isbn=9781580051958 }}</ref> The rate of incarcerated women has expanded at about 4.6% annually between 1995 and 2005 with women now accounting for 7% of the population in state and federal prisons.

[[International Centre for Prison Studies]]. [[International Centre for Prison Studies]]. [[International Centre for Prison Studies]]. Accessed January 8, 2023.</ref> and Sweden is 74 per 100,000 (as of January 2022).<ref name="Sweden">[http://www.prisonstudies.org/country/sweden Sweden]. [[International Centre for Prison Studies]]. Accessed January 8, 2023.</ref>

== Causes ==
{{Further|Crime in the United States}}
[[File:United States correctional population.svg|thumb|300px|Correctional populations in the United States 1980–2013]]
[[File:USA 2009. Percent of adult males incarcerated by race and ethnicity.svg|thumb|300px|2009. Percent of adult males incarcerated by race and ethnicity.<ref>[http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=1006 Prison Inmates at Midyear 2009 – Statistical Tables] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130303174105/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=1006 |date=March 3, 2013 }} (NCJ 230113). [[U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics]]. The rates are for adult males, and are from Tables 18 and 19 of the [http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/pjim06.pdf PDF file] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111027141258/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/pjim06.pdf |date=October 27, 2011 }}. Rates per 100,000 were converted to percentages.</ref>]]
A 2014 report by the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]] identified two main causes of the increase in the United States' incarceration rate over the previous 40 years: longer prison sentences and increases in the likelihood of imprisonment. The same report found that longer prison sentences were the main driver of increasing incarceration rates since 1990.<ref>{{cite book | url=http://www.nap.edu/read/18613/chapter/5 | title=The Growth of Incarceration in the United States: Exploring Causes and Consequences | publisher=National Research Council| author=Travis, Jeremy | year=2014 | pages=40| doi=10.17226/18613 | isbn=978-0-309-29801-8 | s2cid=155470810 }}</ref>

=== Increased sentencing laws ===
{{Further|Three-strikes law}}

Even though there are other countries that commit more inmates to prison annually, the fact that the United States keeps their prisoners longer causes the total rate to become higher. To give an example, the average burglary sentence in the United States is 16 months, compared to 5 months in Canada and 7 months in England.<ref name=liptak>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/23/us/23prison.html?pagewanted=print | work=The New York Times | title=Inmate Count in U.S. Dwarfs Other Nations' | first=Adam | last=Liptak | date=April 23, 2008 | access-date=2010-05-26}}</ref>

Looking at reasons for imprisonment will further clarify why the incarceration rate and length of sentences are so high. The practice of imposing longer prison sentences on repeat offenders is common in many countries, but the [[three-strikes law]]s in the U.S. with mandatory 25-year imprisonment{{px2}}{{mdash}}{{spaces|2|hair}}imple{{shy}}mented in many states in the 1990s{{px2}}{{mdash}}{{spaces|2|hair}}are statutes enacted by state governments in the United States which mandate state courts to impose harsher sentences on habitual offenders who are previously convicted of two prior serious criminal offenses and then commit a third.{{Citation needed|date=April 2019}}

The [[Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act]] of 1994 may have had a minor effect on mass incarceration.<ref>{{cite news |title=The controversial 1994 crime law that Joe Biden helped write, explained |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2019/6/20/18677998/joe-biden-1994-crime-bill-law-mass-incarceration |work=Vox |date=June 20, 2019}}</ref>

=== Economic and age contributions ===
Crime rates in low-income areas are much higher than in middle to high class areas. As a result, incarceration rates in low-income areas are much higher than in wealthier areas due to these high crime rates.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.hamiltonproject.org/papers/ten_economic_facts_about_crime_and_incarceration_in_the_united_states|title=Ten Economic Facts about Crime and Incarceration in the United States {{!}} The Hamilton Project|website=www.hamiltonproject.org|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref> When the incarcerated or criminal is a youth, there is a significant impact on the individual and rippling effects on entire communities. Social capital is lost when an individual is incarcerated. How much social capital is lost is hard to accurately estimate, however Aizer and Doyle found a strong positive correlation between lower income as an adult if an individual is incarcerated in their youth in comparison to those who are not incarcerated.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Aizer|first1=Anna|last2=Doyle|first2=Joseph J.|date=February 2, 2015|title=Juvenile Incarceration, Human Capital, and Future Crime: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges*|url=http://qje.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2015/04/11/qje.qjv003|journal=The Quarterly Journal of Economics|volume=130|issue=2|language=en|pages=759–803|doi=10.1093/qje/qjv003|issn=0033-5533|hdl=1721.1/97380|s2cid=10465708|hdl-access=free}}</ref> 63 percent to 66 percent of those involved in crimes are under the age of thirty.<ref name=":0" /> People incarcerated at a younger age lose the capability to invest in themselves and in their communities.  Their children and families become susceptible to financial burden preventing them from escaping low-income communities. This contributes to the recurring [[cycle of poverty]] that is positively correlated with incarceration.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mosley|first1=Paul|last2=Verschoor|first2=Arjan|date=March 1, 2005|title=Risk Attitudes and the 'Vicious Circle of Poverty'|journal=The European Journal of Development Research|volume=17|issue=1|pages=59–88|doi=10.1080/09578810500066548|s2cid=39514757|issn=0957-8811}}</ref>  Poverty rates have not been curbed despite steady economic growth. Poverty is not the sole dependent variable for increasing incarceration rates. Incarceration leads to more incarceration by putting families and communities at a dynamic social disadvantage.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cj7RCwAAQBAJ&q=mass+incarceration+leads+to+more+incarceration&pg=PR17|title=Imprisoning Communities: How Mass Incarceration Makes Disadvantaged Neighborhoods Worse|last=Clear|first=Todd R.|date=March 27, 2009|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780199728237|language=en}}</ref>

=== Drug sentencing laws ===
[[File:U.S. incarceration rate since 1925.svg|thumb|300px|U.S. prisoners (excluding jails) as a percent of the population: male (dashed red), combined (solid black), female (dotted green)]]
The "[[war on drugs]]" is a policy that was initiated by [[Richard Nixon]] with the [[Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970]] and vigorously pursued by [[Ronald Reagan]].<ref name=JC>{{cite book|last=Alexander|first=Michelle|title=The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindess|year=2010|publisher=The New Press|location=New York|page=52}}</ref> By 2010, drug offenders in federal prison had increased to 500,000 per year, up from 41,000 in 1985. According to [[Michelle Alexander]], drug related charges accounted for more than half the rise in state prisoners between 1985 and 2000. 31 million people have been arrested on drug related charges, approximately 1 in 10 Americans.<ref>{{cite book|last=Alexander|first=Michelle|title=The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness|year=2010|publisher=The New Press|location=New York|page=60}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Shackles Beyond the Sentence: How Legal Financial Obligations Create a Permanent Underclass|ssrn = 2628977|publisher = Social Science Research Network|date = July 9, 2015|location = Rochester, NY|last = SpearIt}}</ref> In contrast, John Pfaff of [[Fordham Law School]] has accused Alexander of exaggerating the influence of the war on drugs on the rise in the United States' incarceration rate: according to him, the percent of state prisoners whose primary offense was drug-related peaked at 22% in 1990.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/crime/2015/02/mass_incarceration_a_provocative_new_theory_for_why_so_many_americans_are.html | title=Why Are So Many Americans in Prison? | work=Slate | date=February 6, 2015 | access-date=February 14, 2016 | author=Neyfakh, Leon}}</ref>  The Brookings Institution reconciles the differences between Alexander and Pfaff by explaining two ways to look at the prison population as it relates to drug crimes, concluding "The picture is clear: Drug crimes have been the predominant reason for new admissions into state and federal prisons in recent decades" and "rolling back the war on drugs would not, as Pfaff and Urban Institute scholars maintain, totally solve the problem of mass incarceration, but it could help a great deal, by reducing exposure to prison."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.brookings.edu/blog/social-mobility-memos/2015/11/25/drug-offenders-in-american-prisons-the-critical-distinction-between-stock-and-flow/ | title=Drug offenders in American prisons: The critical distinction between stock and flow | work=Brookings | date=November 25, 2015 | access-date=September 1, 2016 | author=Rothwell, Jonathan}}</ref>

As of December 2017, only 14.4% of state prisoners were serving sentences for a drug offenses with 3.7% of serving for possession and 10.8% serving for trafficking, other drug offenses, and unspecified drug offenses.<ref>{{cite web |author1=E. Ann Carson |title=Prisoners in 2018 |url=https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/p18.pdf |publisher=U.S. Department of Justice, Bureau of Justice Statistics |access-date=July 8, 2022 |location=Table 13 |page=21 |language=English }}</ref> Time served for drug related offenses are also among the shortest with prisoners released in 2016 having served an average sentence length 22 months while the median time served only 14 months.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Danielle Kaeble |title=Time Served in State Prison, 2016 |url=https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/tssp16.pdf | publisher=U.S. Department of Justice, Bureau of Justice Statistics | access-date=July 8, 2022 |location=Table 1 |page=2 |date=November 2018}}</ref>

After the passage of Reagan's Anti-Drug Abuse Act in 1986, incarceration for non-violent offenses dramatically increased.  The Act imposed the same five-year [[mandatory sentencing|mandatory sentence]] on those with convictions involving crack as on those possessing 100 times as much powder cocaine.<ref name=JC /><ref name="Lyons">{{cite web|last=Lyons|first=John|title=War on the Family: Mothers in Prison and the Children They Leave Behind|work=DVD|publisher=Peace Productions}}</ref> This had a disproportionate effect on low-level street dealers and users of crack, who were more commonly poor blacks, Latinos, the young, and women.<ref>{{cite book|last=Golden|first=Renny|title=War on the Family: Mothers in Prison and the Families They Leave Behind|url=https://archive.org/details/waronfamilymothe0000gold|url-access=registration|year=2005|publisher=Routledge|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/waronfamilymothe0000gold/page/45 45]}}</ref>

Courts were given more discretion in sentencing by the ''[[Kimbrough v. United States]]'' (2007) decision, and the disparity was decreased to 18:1 by the [[Fair Sentencing Act of 2010]].<ref name=famm>[http://www.famm.org/FederalSentencing/USCongress/BillsinCongress/TheFairSentencingActof2010.aspx "Fair Sentencing Act of 2010"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303203132/http://www.famm.org/FederalSentencing/USCongress/BillsinCongress/TheFairSentencingActof2010.aspx |date=March 3, 2012 }}, Families Against Mandatory Minimums, famm.org. Retrieved September 30, 2010.</ref>

By 2003, 58% of all women in federal prison were convicted of drug offenses.<ref>[[Bureau of Justice Statistics]]. Sourcebook of Criminal Justice Statistics Online (30th ed.). 2002. ''Cited in'' [https://www.aclu.org/womens-rights/words-prison-did-you-know#_edn13 "Words From Prison – Did You Know...?"], [[American Civil Liberties Union]], June 12, 2006.</ref>  Black and Hispanic women in particular have been disproportionately affected by the war on drugs. Since 1986, incarceration rates have risen by 400% for women of all races, while rates for Black women have risen by 800%.<ref>Marc Mauer, Cathy Potler & Richard Wolf, Gender and Justice: Women, Drugs, and Sentencing Policy, [[The Sentencing Project]]. November 1997. ''Cited in'' [https://www.aclu.org/womens-rights/words-prison-did-you-know#_edn13 "Words From Prison – Did You Know...?"], [[American Civil Liberties Union]], June 12, 2006, and {{cite web|title=Caught in the Net: Impact of Drug Policies on Women and Families|url=https://www.aclu.org/files/images/asset_upload_file431_23513.pdf|publisher=American Civil Liberties Union|access-date=April 15, 2011}}</ref> Formerly incarcerated Black women are also most negatively impacted by the collateral legal consequences of conviction.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = The Modern Day Scarlet Letter|ssrn = 2460898|date = 2015|location = 83 Fordham L. Rev. 2999 (2015)|first = Ifeoma|last = Ajunwa}}</ref>

According to the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], "Even when  women have minimal or no involvement in the drug trade, they are increasingly caught in the ever-widening net cast by current drug laws, through provisions of the criminal law such as those involving [[Conspiracy (crime)|conspiracy]], [[accomplice liability]], and [[constructive possession]] that expand [[criminal liability]] to reach partners, relatives and bystanders."<ref>"[https://www.aclu.org/womens-rights/words-prison-did-you-know#_edn13 Words From Prison – Did You Know...?]", [[American Civil Liberties Union]], June 12, 2006.</ref>

These new policies also disproportionately affect African-American women. According to [[Dorothy E. Roberts]], the explanation is that poor women, who are disproportionately black, are more likely to be placed under constant supervision by the State to receive social services.<ref>{{cite book|last=Roberts|first=Dorothy|title=[[Killing the Black Body: Race, Reproduction, and the Meaning of Liberty]]|year=1997|publisher=Vintage Books|location=New York|page=172}}</ref> They are then more likely to be caught by officials who are instructed to look specifically for drug offenses. Roberts argues that the criminal justice system's creation of new crimes has a direct effect on the number of women, especially black women, who then become incarcerated.{{Citation needed|date=April 2019}}

===Racialization ===
{{See also|Race in the United States criminal justice system}}
One of the first laws in the U.S. against drugs was the [[Smoking Opium Exclusion Act of 1909]]. It prohibited the smoking of opium, which was ingested but not smoked by a substantial portion of White housewives in the United States. It was smoked mainly by Asian American immigrants coming to build the railroads. These immigrants were targeted with anti-Asian sentiment, as many voters believed they were losing jobs to Asian immigrants.{{citation needed|date=October 2017}}

==== Disproportionate incarceration of black and Hispanic people ====
{{see also|Race and crime in the United States}}
In the early 2000s, the U.S. was at its highest rate of imprisonment in history,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Western, Pettit|first=Bruce, Becky|date=2010|title=Incarceration & Social Inequality|journal=Dædalus|volume=139|issue=3|pages=8–19|doi=10.1162/daed_a_00019|pmid=21032946|s2cid=57571604|doi-access=free}}</ref> with young Black men experiencing the highest levels of incarceration. One out of every 15 people imprisoned across the world is a Black American incarcerated in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prisonstudies.org/sites/default/files/resources/downloads/wppl_12.pdf |date=2018 | title=World Prison Population List |work=World Prison Brief, Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research |access-date=January 29, 2022}}</ref> A 2004 study reported that the majority of people sentenced to prison in the United States are Black, and almost one-third of Black men in their twenties are either on parole, on probation, or in prison.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Roberts|first=Dorothy|date=2004|title=The Social and Moral Cost of Mass Incarceration in African American Communities|journal=Stanford Law Review}}</ref> These disproportionate levels of imprisonment have made incarceration a normalized occurrence for [[African Americans|African-American]] communities. This has resulted in distrust from Black individuals towards aspects of the legal system such as police, courts, and heavy sentences.<ref name=":1" /> In 2011, more than 580,000 Black men and women were in state or federal prison.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Brewer|first=Russell|date=Spring 2014|title=The High Prevalence of Incarceration History Among Black Men Who Have Sex With Men in the United States: Associations and Implications|journal=American Journal of Public Health|volume=104|issue=3|pages=448–454|pmc=3953792|doi=10.2105/ajph.2013.301786|pmid=24432948}}</ref> Black men and women are imprisoned at higher rates compared to all other age groups, with the highest rate being Black men aged 25 to 39. In 2001, almost 17% of Black men had previously been imprisoned in comparison to 2.6% of White men. By the end of 2002, of the two million inmates of the U.S. incarceration system, Black men surpassed the number of White men (586,700 to 436,800 respectively of inmates with sentences more than one year).<ref name=":1" /> Becky Petit and Carmen Gutierrez performed a study, published on October 29, 2018, on the incarceration rate of young African Americans, noting that 48.9% of men arrested by age 23 (born 1980–1984), were African American, while 37.9% were white.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pettit |first1=Becky |last2=Gutierrez |first2=Carmen |date=May 2018 |title=Mass Incarceration and Racial Inequality |journal=The American Journal of Economics and Sociology |language=en |volume=77 |issue=3–4 |pages=1153–1182 |doi=10.1111/ajes.12241 |issn=0002-9246 |pmc=9540942 |pmid=36213171}}</ref>

However, in the 21st century, the incarceration rates for African American and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic American]] women have declined, while incarceration rates have increased for [[White Americans|white women]]. Between 2000 and 2017, the incarceration rate for white women increased by 44%, while at the same time declining by 55% for African American women.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sultan |first1=Bonnie |last2=Myrent |first2=Mark |title=Women and Girls in Corrections |url=https://www.jrsa.org/pubs/factsheets/jrsa-factsheet-women-girls-in-corrections.pdf |publisher=Justice Research and Statistics Association (JRSA) |access-date=August 27, 2023 |archive-date=August 27, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230827191109/https://www.jrsa.org/pubs/factsheets/jrsa-factsheet-women-girls-in-corrections.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The Sentencing Project reports that by 2021, incarceration rates had declined by 70% for African American women, while rising by 7% for white women.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Budd |first1=Kristen |title=Incarcerated Women and Girls |url=https://www.sentencingproject.org/fact-sheet/incarcerated-women-and-girls/ |website=The Sentencing Project |date=April 3, 2023}}</ref>

In 2017, the [[Washington Post]] reported that [[White American|white]] women's incarceration rate was growing faster than ever before, as the rate for black women declined.<ref name="Humphreys 2017 x017">{{cite news | last=Humphreys | first=Keith | title=White women are going to prison at a higher rate than ever before | newspaper=Washington Post | date=January 24, 2017 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2017/01/24/white-women-are-going-to-prison-at-a-higher-rate-than-ever-before/ | access-date=2023-08-27}}</ref> The incarceration rate of African American males is also falling sharply, even faster than white men's incarceration rate, contrary to the popular opinion that black males are increasingly incarcerated.<ref name="Lane 2023 y855">{{cite news | last=Lane | first=Charles | title=New data show a dire forecast about incarceration rates didn't come true | newspaper=Washington Post | date=July 12, 2023 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2023/07/12/good-news-black-incarceration-rate-declines/ | access-date=2023-08-27}}</ref>

The war on drugs played a role in the disproportionate amount of incarcerated African-Americans.<ref name=":1" /> Despite a general decline in crime, the massive increase in new inmates due to drug offenses ensured historically high incarceration rates during the 1990s, with New York City serving as an example. Drug-related arrests continued to increase in the city despite a near 50% drop in felony crimes.

A significant contributing factor to these figures are the racially and economically segregated neighborhoods that account for the majority of the Black prison population. These neighborhoods are normally impoverished and possess a high minority population. For example, as many as one in eight adult males who inhabit these urban areas is sent to prison each year, and one in four of these men is in prison on any given day. A 1992 study revealed that 72% of all New York State's prisoners came from only 7 of New York City's 55 [[Community boards of New York City|community districts]]. Upon release from prison, the most common area that African Americans return to is a poor, impoverished neighborhood.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crutchfield |first=Robert D. |date=November 6, 2023 |title=The Effects of Mass Incarceration on Communities – ProQuest |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/1774763408 |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=The Effects of Mass Incarceration on Communities of Color |id={{ProQuest|1774763408}} |language=en}}</ref>

Finding employment post-release is a significant struggle for African Americans.<ref name=":2" /> American sociologist [[Devah Pager]] performed a study to prove this. She assembled pairs of fake job seekers to find jobs with résumés that portrayed the applicant had a criminal record. The findings indicated that the presence of a criminal record reduced callbacks by approximately 50%. [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic women]] with a prison record fared most favorably in receiving a phone call back from potential employers, while African American women had modest results, with [[White Americans|white women]] receiving the poorest results, obtaining the lowest probability of receiving a phone call from a potential employer.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/p13.pdf|title=Prisoners in 2013|last=Carson|first=E. Ann|publisher=U.S. Department of Justice|year=2014|pages=36–37, 39}} "'''Pages 36–37:''' White women have odds of receiving a favorable response from hiring managers that are nearly 50 percent smaller than the odds of Hispanic women with a prison record, the odds of white women with a prison record are only five percent smaller than black women’s with a prison record. '''Page 39:''' More than half—52 percent—of the positive outcomes observed during the audit benefitted the employment prospects of Hispanic women. White women received 36 percent of favorable responses. A complete breakdown of the  distribution of favorable responses is reported in Table 3."</ref>

Unemployment rates impacted the body of African Americans that would take up prisons. The young African Americans who have found themselves as unemployed are found to be incarcerated at a higher rate than unemployed white people, as a result of drug usage.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Western |first1=Bruce |last2=Wildeman |first2=Christopher |date=January 2009 |title=The Black Family and Mass Incarceration |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0002716208324850 |journal=The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science |language=en |volume=621 |issue=1 |pages=221–242 |doi=10.1177/0002716208324850 |s2cid=53870729 |issn=0002-7162|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Prison privatization===
In the 1980s, the rising number of people incarcerated as a result of the war on drugs and the wave of privatization that occurred under the [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|Reagan administration]] saw the emergence of the for-profit prison industry. Although modern [[private prison]]s did not exist in the US prior to the 1980s,<ref>Khalek, Rania. [http://www.salon.com/2011/12/01/how_private_prisons_game_the_system/ How private prisons game the system]. Salon.com. December 1, 2011.</ref><ref>[[Bernard Harcourt|Harcourt, Bernard]] (2012). ''[http://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674066168 The Illusion of Free Markets: Punishment and the Myth of Natural Order].'' [[Harvard University Press]]. {{ISBN|0674066162}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=LW8I66EGmfcC&q=GEO%20Group&pg=PA235 p. 235]</ref><ref>Selman, Donna and Paul Leighton (2010). ''[https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/punishment-for-sale-9781442201729/ Punishment for Sale: Private Prisons, Big Business, and the Incarceration Binge] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190813111821/https://rowman.com/ISBN/9781442201729/Punishment-for-Sale-Private-Prisons-Big-Business-and-the-Incarceration-Binge |date=August 13, 2019 }}.'' Rowman & Littlefield Publishers. {{ISBN|1442201738}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=5lBraTDtiSgC&pg=PR11 p. xi]</ref> the concept of private prisons can be found within the United States as early as the 1800s.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|date=September 23, 2020|title=Capital and the Carceral State: Prison Privatization in the United States and United Kingdom|url=https://hir.harvard.edu/us-uk-prison-privatization/|access-date=2021-07-06|website=Harvard International Review|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite magazine|title=America's Shocking History of Private Prisons|url=https://time.com/5405158/the-true-history-of-americas-private-prison-industry/|access-date=2021-07-06|magazine=Time|language=en}}</ref> In 1844, Louisiana privatized its penitentiary when it allowed a private company to run the facility as a factory where prisoners were used to manufacture clothing.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

In a 2011 report by the ACLU, it is claimed that the rise of the for-profit prison industry is a "major contributor" to "[[mass incarceration]]," along with bloated state budgets.<ref name="Shapiro">{{cite web|last=Shapiro|first=David|title=Banking on Bondage: Private Prisons and Mass Incarceration|url=https://www.aclu.org/files/assets/bankingonbondage_20111102.pdf|publisher=[[American Civil Liberties Union]]|access-date=March 31, 2013}}</ref> Louisiana, for example, has the highest rate of incarceration in the world with the majority of its prisoners being housed in privatized, for-profit facilities. Such institutions could face bankruptcy without a steady influx of prisoners.<ref>{{cite news|last=Chang|first=Cindy|title=Louisiana is the world's prison capital|url=http://www.nola.com/crime/index.ssf/2012/05/louisiana_is_the_worlds_prison.html|newspaper=[[The Times-Picayune]]|date=May 29, 2012|access-date=April 4, 2013}}</ref> A 2013 Bloomberg report states that in the past decade the number of inmates in for-profit prisons throughout the U.S. rose 44 percent.<ref>Margaret Newkirk & William Selway (July 12, 2013). [https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-07-12/gangs-ruled-prison-as-for-profit-model-put-blood-on-floor.html "Gangs Ruled Prison as For-Profit Model Put Blood on Floor."] [[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]. Retrieved July 16, 2013.</ref>

Corporations who operate prisons, such as [[CoreCivic]] (formerly the Corrections Corporation of America) and the [[GEO Group]], spend significant amounts of money lobbying the federal government along with state governments.<ref name="Shapiro"/> The two aforementioned companies, the largest in the industry, have been contributors to the [[American Legislative Exchange Council]] (ALEC), which seeks to expand the privatization of corrections and lobbies for policies that would increase incarceration, such as three-strike laws and "truth-in-sentencing" legislation.<ref>Elk, Mike and Sloan, Bob (2011). [http://www.thenation.com/article/162478/hidden-history-alec-and-prison-labor The Hidden History of ALEC and Prison Labor]. ''[[The Nation]]''.</ref><ref>[http://www.sentencingproject.org/Admin/Documents/publications/inc_prisonprivatization.pdf Prison Privatization and the Use of Incarceration]. The Sentencing Project, September 2004. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070714063407/http://www.sentencingproject.org/Admin/Documents/publications/inc_prisonprivatization.pdf |date=July 14, 2007 }}</ref><ref name="Rutherford">{{cite news|url=https://www.rutherford.org/publications_resources/john_whiteheads_commentary/jailing_americans_for_profit_the_rise_of_the_prison_industrial_complex|title=Jailing Americans for Profit: The Rise of the Prison Industrial Complex|last=Whitehead|first=John|date=April 10, 2012|publisher=[[The Rutherford Institute]]|access-date=April 2, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Sullivan, Laura">Sullivan, Laura (2010). [https://www.npr.org/2010/10/28/130833741/prison-economics-help-drive-ariz-immigration-law Prison Economics Help Drive Ariz. Immigration Law]. ''[[National Public Radio]]''.</ref><ref>Pat Beall (November 22, 2013). [http://www.mypalmbeachpost.com/news/news/big-business-group-behind-push-that-filled-florida/nbYTc/ Big business, legislators pushed for stiff sentences]. ''[[The Palm Beach Post]].'' Retrieved November 10, 2014.</ref><ref>Marie Gottschalk. ''[http://press.princeton.edu/titles/10731.html Caught: The Prison State and the Lockdown of American Politics].'' Princeton University Press, 2014. [https://books.google.com/books?id=iOs_BAAAQBAJ&pg=PA61 p. 61]</ref> Prison companies also sign contracts with states that guarantee at least 90 percent of prison beds be filled. If these "lockup quotas" are not met, the state must reimburse the prison company for the unused beds. Prison companies use the profits to expand and put pressure on lawmakers to incarcerate a certain number of people.<ref>Katy Hall and Jan Diehm (September 19, 2013). [http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/09/19/private-prisons_n_3955686.html One Disturbing Reason For Our Exploding Prison Population (INFOGRAPHIC)]. ''[[The Huffington Post]]'' Retrieved September 20, 2013.</ref><ref>[http://www.inthepublicinterest.org/sites/default/files/Criminal%20Lockup%20Quota%20Report.pdf CRIMINAL: How Lockup Quotas and "Low-Crime Taxes" Guarantee Profits for Private Prison Corporations] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140424045843/http://www.inthepublicinterest.org/sites/default/files/Criminal%20Lockup%20Quota%20Report.pdf |date=April 24, 2014 }}. ''In the Public Interest.'' Retrieved September 20, 2013.</ref> This influence on the government by the private prison industry has been referred to as the [[prison–industrial complex]].<ref name="Rutherford"/>

The industry is well aware of what reduced crime rates could mean to their bottom line. This from the CCA's SEC report in 2010:

<blockquote>Our growth … depends on a number of factors we cannot control, including crime rates … [R]eductions in crime rates … could lead to reductions in arrests, convictions and sentences requiring incarceration at correctional facilities.<ref name="Shapiro"/></blockquote>In January 2021, U.S. President [[Joe Biden]] signed an executive order directing the [[Department of Justice]] (DOJ) to begin phasing out its contracts with private federal prisons.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 29, 2021|title=Reforming Our Incarceration System To Eliminate the Use of Privately Operated Criminal Detention Facilities|url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/01/29/2021-02070/reforming-our-incarceration-system-to-eliminate-the-use-of-privately-operated-criminal-detention|access-date=2021-07-06|website=Federal Register}}</ref>

As of March 2021, the private prison population of the United States has seen a 16% decline since reaching its peak in 2012 with 137,000 people incarcerated.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|title=Private Prisons in the United States|url=https://www.sentencingproject.org/publications/private-prisons-united-states/|access-date=2021-07-06|website=The Sentencing Project|language=en-US}}</ref> According to a March 2021 report released by [[The Sentencing Project]], 115,428 people were incarcerated in private prisons in the US, representing 8% of the total state and federal prison population.<ref name=":6" />

===Editorial policies of major media===
{{see also|Strategic lawsuit against public participation}}

Gallup polling since 1989 has found that in most years in which there was a decline in the U.S. crime rate, a majority of Americans said that violent crime was getting worse.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/150464/americans-believe-crime-worsening.aspx|title=Most Americans Believe Crime in U.S. Is Worsening|author=Gallup, Inc.|work=Gallup.com|date=October 31, 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/179546/americans-crime-last-year.aspx|title=Most Americans Still See Crime Up Over Last Year|author=Gallup, Inc.|work=Gallup.com|date=November 21, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gallup.com/poll/165653/crime-americans-seem-noticed.aspx|title=U.S. Crime Is Up, but Americans Don't Seem to Have Noticed|author=Gallup, Inc.|work=Gallup.com|date=October 31, 2013 }}</ref>

A substantial body of research claims that incarceration rates are primarily a function of media editorial policies, largely unrelated to the actual crime rate. ''Constructing Crime: Perspectives on Making News and Social Problems'' is a book collecting together papers on this theme.<ref>Potter and Kapeller (1998)</ref> The researchers say that the jump in incarceration rate from 0.1% to 0.5% of the United States population from 1975 to 2000 (documented in the figure above) was driven by changes in the editorial policies of the mainstream commercial media and is unrelated to any actual changes in crime. [[Media consolidation]] reduced competition on content. That allowed media company executives to maintain substantially the same audience while slashing budgets for investigative journalism and filling the space from the police blotter, which tended to increase and stabilize advertising revenue. It is safer, easier and cheaper to write about crimes committed by poor people than the wealthy. Poor people can be libeled with impunity, but major advertisers can materially impact the profitability of a commercial media organization by reducing their purchases of advertising space with that organization.

News media thrive on [[Media feeding frenzy|feeding frenzies]] (such as [[Missing white woman syndrome|missing white women]]) because they tend to reduce production costs while simultaneously building an audience interested in the latest development in a particular story. It takes a long time for a reporter to learn enough to write intelligently about a specific issue. Once a reporter has achieved that level of knowledge, it is easier to write subsequent stories. However, major advertisers have been known to spend their advertising budgets through different channels when they dislike the editorial policies. Therefore, a media feeding frenzy focusing on an issue of concern to an advertiser may reduce revenue and profits.<ref name='McChesney2004'>McChesney (2004, p. 81) wrote, "A five-year study of investigative journalism on TV news completed in 2002 determined that investigative journalism has all but disappeared from the nation's commercial airwaves."</ref>

Sacco described how "competing news organizations responded to each other's coverage [while] the police, in their role as gatekeepers of crime news, reacted to the increased media interest by making available more stories that reflected and reinforced" a particular theme.  "[T]he dynamics of competitive journalism created a media feeding frenzy that found news workers 'snatching at shocking numbers' and 'smothering reports of stable or decreasing use under more ominous headlines.'"<ref>{{Citation 
| last = Sacco | first = Vincent F. 
| date=May 1995 | title = Media Constructions of Crime 
| journal = Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science 
| volume = 539 | pages = 141–154| doi = 10.1177/0002716295539001011 
| s2cid = 145187502 
}}, reprinted as chapter 2 of Potter and Kapeller (1998, pp. 37-51, esp. p. 42)</ref>

The reasons cited above for increased incarcerations (US racial demographics, Increased sentencing laws, and Drug sentencing laws) have been described as consequences of the shift in editorial policies of the mainstream media.<ref>See also {{cite book|last1=Sacco|first1=Vincent F|title=When Crime Waves|date=2005|publisher=Sage|isbn=978-0761927839}} and {{cite book|last1=Youngblood|first1=Steven|title=Peace Journalism Principles and Practices|date=2017|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-138-12467-7|pages=115–131}}</ref>

Additionally, media coverage has been proven to have a profound impact on criminal sentencing. [[Sara Sun Beale|Beale]] found that the more media attention a criminal case is given, the greater the incentive for prosecutors and judges to pursue harsher sentences.<ref name='Beale'><!-- Beale (2006) The News Media's Influence on Criminal Justice Policy: How Market-Driven News Promotes Punitiveness -->{{cite Q|Q106450992}}</ref> This is directly linked to the enormous increase in media coverage of crime over the past two decades.<ref>Potter and Kapeller (1998).</ref> While crime decreased by 8% between 1992 and 2002, news reports on crime increased by 800% and the average prison sentence length increased by 2,000% for all crimes.{{Citation needed|date=February 2019}} Less media coverage means a greater chance of a lighter sentence or that the defendant may avoid prison time entirely.<ref name='Beale' />
